## Why Plan Mode isnât enough

For a long while, my default move with any non-trivial feature was Claude Codeâs plan mode. Sketch the idea, let it draft a plan, skim it, hit go.

The cracks showed up fast.

- A fuzzy ask produces a fuzzy plan. The output looks structured and confident, but itâs quietly inheriting every gap in your thinking.

- The agent drifts mid-execution. You approve a plan, switch to execute, and it quietly adds files and patterns the plan never mentioned. You end up appending âimplement exactly as written, nothing extraâ to every run.

- It never challenges the idea itself. Plan mode answers how Claude would build your thing. It never asks whether the thing is worth building, or whether youâve actually thought it through. You can burn three days producing a clean, well-structured mistake.

That last one is the real gap. Plan mode assumes your idea is already sound and your only problem is execution. Most of the time, that assumption is wrong â and thatâs the exact gap /grill-me fills.

The whole thing runs as a single continuous session, each step feeding the next.

The rule that makes it work: never /clear between steps. The PRD skill leans on everything from the grill â your answers, your reasoning, the edge cases you named, the trade-offs you accepted. A PRD generated cold is a template. A PRD generated right after a grill is a spec with a point of view.

Tight PRD in, tight tickets out â /to-issues produces tasks with real context and acceptance criteria, not âimplement auth.â Tight tickets mean /afk can execute without guessing.

Thereâs a second payoff that shows up later. The PRD and the issues are written artifacts â they live in your tracker, not just in a chat window. So when a session dies halfway, or you come back to the same feature a week later, youâre not reconstructing intent from memory. You point a fresh session at the PRD and the open issues, and it picks up with the full reasoning already in hand: what you decided, why, and whatâs left. The grill happens once; the context it produces keeps paying out across every session that touches the feature.

> Output quality at the end is a direct function of honesty at the beginning.

## When the grill gets hard: /handoff

Deep grill sessions burn context. Youâre well into one when you realize you need to prototype something or check how an existing schema behaves. The instinct is to do it right there in the same session.

Donât.

Pocock also wrote /handoff , built for exactly this. It compresses the current session into a document a fresh agent can pick up â context, decisions, intent, suggested next steps. Your grill stays clean; the side quest gets its own window.

Two patterns:

- Fire and forget â something out of scope appears. Hand it to a fresh agent, return to the grill.

- Grill â handoff â prototype â handoff back â validate an assumption in a throwaway session, bring the learning home.

The harder the questions, the more context a grill accumulates â and the more valuable it becomes to protect it. /handoff is how you keep going hard without drowning the session.

> The deeper the grill, the more there is to lose by derailing it. A handoff lets you chase a tangent and come back to a session thatâs still sharp.

## Beyond the grill: getting Claude Code to run lean

The grill is the star of the workflow, but it only pays off if the rest of your setup isnât quietly bleeding tokens and context. These are the habits that keep Claude Code fast, cheap, and sharp around it.

Run grill sessions on the strongest model; implement on a cheaper one.

A grill is pure exploration â no file writes, no tool-call overhead â so a frontier model like Opus earns its cost here by asking sharper questions and catching contradictions a smaller model misses, and the token bill stays low because itâs just conversation. Once you cross into implementation â /afk , /tdd , execution â a model like Sonnet does the heavy lifting at a fraction of the price.

> Spend your best model where decisions are made, not where code is typed.

.claudeignore cuts your context bill in one edit.

By default Claude pulls everything in your project into scope. A .claudeignore file (same syntax as .gitignore ) stops the dead weight from auto-loading â excluding .next/ alone can trim 30â40% off context in a Next.js repo. Itâs the highest-leverage two minutes youâll spend.

node_modules/ dist/ build/ .next/ __pycache__/ *.lock .git/ *.db

This doesnât stop Claude from reading these files when you explicitly ask â it just keeps them out of automatic exploration.

Keep files under 200â300 lines.

Agents read whole files. When one reads a 1,500-line file to find a 20-line function, it pays for 1,480 lines of noise â and reasons worse for it. This isnât a prompt trick; itâs a codebase discipline that compounds across every read in a session.

> A large file is a tax every agent pays, every time it looks.

Teach Claude to grep, not read â in CLAUDE.md .

CLAUDE.md is the one file Claude reads at the start of every session, so itâs where your projectâs standing rules live â stack, conventions, and the things you never want to re-explain. The highest-value rule you can put there: tell it which files to search instead of read . We have a translation-keys file with over 2,000 entries; reading it whole would torch the context budget on noise. So CLAUDE.md says:

grep in `packages/survey-type-defs/src/appTranslation/AppTranslationKeyEnum.ts` â 2000+ keys, never read the full file

One line, and Claude stops pulling a giant file into context every time it needs a single key. Do this for every oversized-but-unavoidable file in your repo.

Disable MCP servers you arenât using.

Historically, Claude Code would load MCP tool definitions directly into context, and a few heavy servers (Playwright, GitHub, Gmail, etc.) could quietly consume thousands of tokens each â and a sprawling setup, tens of thousands per turn. Recent Claude Code versions mitigate this with Tool Search, now enabled by default: tools are discovered and loaded on demand instead of shipping every schema upfront. It helps, but large MCP setups still add overhead and complexity. Run /context to inspect what each server is costing you, and prune unused servers with /mcp .

Compact early â around half-full, not when it breaks.

Quality degrades as the window fills; by the time responses feel hazy, youâre already deep in the rot zone. The practical sweet spot is compacting around 50â60% capacity, while Claude still has full, uncompressed context to summarize from. Waiting until 90% means youâre summarizing an already-degraded view.

Git worktrees for parallel agents.

Independent features donât need to run one after another. Worktrees give each agent its own branch and isolated directory off the same repo, so three agents can do in an hour what would take three sequentially â no context collisions, no merge chaos.

The shape of building software has flipped.

Writing code used to be the bottleneck â now itâs the part agents are best at. Whatâs left for us is deciding whatâs actually worth building and being precise enough that the implementation doesnât drift.

Thatâs why the highest-leverage skill in this workflow is /grill-me â a skill that generates no code at all, yet creates more leverage than anything else.

Everything else â lean context, smaller files, the right model for the right phase â is just there to protect that thinking from noise.
